interest: This file provides exceptional insight into Japan's remilitarization and administrative consolidation of the Kwantung Leased Territory following the Mukden Incident and the creation of Manchukuo. It illuminates how the Imperial Japanese Navy navigated the intersection of military base expansion, strategic defense, and commercial maritime law, specifically balancing closed military zones against foreign commercial access to the Western Harbor and naval dry docks. The despatches of future prominent diplomat John Carter Vincent showcase the methods and diplomatic caution of American consular intelligence-gathering under Japanese rule. Furthermore, the documents capture international friction surrounding Japanese expansionism, documenting British diplomatic concern over potential violations of the Nine-Power Treaty and naval limitation frameworks.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.34594C) documents the re-establishment of the Imperial Japanese Navy's secondary naval station and naval depot at Port Arthur (Lüshun) in the Kwantung Leased Territory during the spring of 1933, following the Japanese invasion of Manchuria and the creation of Manchukuo. Compiled primarily through despatches from American Consul John Carter Vincent in Dairen to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo, the file contains official translations of the revised Port Arthur port regulations (Naval Department Ordinance No. 2), an annotated harbor map detailing restricted naval zones and the commercial Western Harbor, and local press clippings from the Manshu Nippo and The Manchuria Daily News detailing organizational rosters, assigned warships, and strategic rationales. The records also include internal State Department memoranda and consular reports clarifying regulatory errata, commercial navigation restrictions, and the availability of naval dry docks operated under contract by the Manchuria Dock Company to foreign merchant shipping.

subfiles.about: Transmits the revised Port Arthur port regulations, an annotated harbor map, and local press reports regarding the re-establishment of the naval station.
subfiles.summary: American Consul John Carter Vincent in Dairen reports to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo on the recent re-establishment of a Japanese naval station at Port Arthur. He encloses an English translation of the revised port regulations (Navy Department Ordinance No. 2) and an annotated photographic harbor map. Vincent notes that Japanese press coverage is more detailed than local Dairen reporting, and explains that he avoided making indiscreet direct official inquiries to naval or Kwantung authorities while enclosing relevant press clippings.
subfiles.title: Despatch from Consul John Carter Vincent to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew on Port Arthur Naval Station

subfiles.about: Sets forth the official naval ordinance and regulatory articles governing maritime zones, entry permits, pilotage, and security restrictions at Port Arthur.
subfiles.summary: Official translation of Navy Department Ordinance No. 2 dividing Port Arthur into three regulatory water zones. The First and Second Areas are reserved strictly for Imperial Japanese Navy vessels, requiring special permission from the Commander-in-Chief for entry, while the Third Area and Western Harbor permit free access to commercial and foreign shipping. The regulations prescribe strict rules regarding ship identification, nationality flags, quarantine, mandatory retired naval pilots for vessels over 1,800 tons, and comprehensive security prohibitions on photography, surveying, sounding, aviation, and wireless telegraphy.
subfiles.title: Kwantung Government Translation of Port Arthur Regulations (Navy Department Ordinance No. 2)

subfiles.about: Delineates the three regulatory harbor zones and navigational boundaries of the Port of Port Arthur.
subfiles.summary: A photographic reproduction of the official hydrographic map accompanying the Port Arthur regulations, showing the layout and jurisdictional divisions of Port Arthur. The American Consulate in Dairen romanized the Japanese place names and added directional arrows to indicate the boundaries of the First, Second, and Third Areas and the Western Harbor. The map illustrates the naval reserve land, coastal topography, and entrance fairway subject to naval control.
subfiles.title: Map of the Port of Port Arthur Showing Harbor Areas

subfiles.about: Reports the revival of the naval station, organizational department structure, personnel appointments, and assigned warships.
subfiles.summary: An extract from the Dairen Japanese-language newspaper Manshu Nippo announcing the re-establishment of the Port Arthur Secondary Naval Station on April 20, 1933, after twelve years, replacing the Second Despatched Squadron. It details the station's departmental structure (Harbor Office, Navy Hospital, Wireless Station) and publishes an officer roster headed by Commander-in-Chief Rear-Admiral Shidzuo Tsuda and Chief Staff-Officer Captain Hisaharu Kubota. It lists assigned warships—including cruisers Hirato and Kuma, aircraft tender Shin-i, and destroyers—and outlines the station's strategic mission to protect 20,000 Japanese residents north of the Yangtze River and defend the Kwantung coast.
subfiles.title: Extract from Manshu Nippo on the Establishment of Port Arthur Secondary Naval Station

subfiles.about: Analyzes the strategic motives behind reopening Port Arthur naval base and responds to international concerns regarding treaty compliance.
subfiles.summary: An editorial by George W. Gorman in the English-language, Japanese-controlled Manchuria Daily News reviewing the strategic rationale behind restoring Port Arthur as an active naval base. Gorman traces the port's status since the Russo-Japanese War and explains its role in defending Manchukuo, patrolling North China waters, protecting northern fisheries, and facilitating warship repairs. Quoting an official Navy Office spokesman, the article discusses the planned recovery of dry docks leased to the Manchuria Dock Company and argues against British diplomatic concerns under the Nine-Power Treaty by asserting the revival is non-offensive and purely for regional defense.
subfiles.title: Editorial by George W. Gorman in The Manchuria Daily News: 'Port Arthur's Revival'

subfiles.about: Summarizes consular reporting on corrections to the Port Arthur regulations and notes foreign commercial access to naval dry docks.
subfiles.summary: An internal Department of State memorandum prepared by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizing Dairen's despatch of May 24, 1933. It confirms that corrections to the Port Arthur port regulations have been incorporated into the translation on file and notes that the Dairen Consulate is translating supplementary Detailed Regulations relevant to American shipping. The memorandum also records that while dry docks in the First Area are omitted from the port regulations, the British Consul was informed that foreign vessels could utilize them upon obtaining permission from the Commander-in-Chief.
subfiles.title: State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Port Arthur Regulations

subfiles.about: Forwards official errata to the Port Arthur regulations, reviews supplementary detailed regulations, and reports on foreign access to dry docks.
subfiles.summary: Consul John Carter Vincent transmits textual corrections issued by the Kwantung Government for Articles 1, 7, 8, 9, 13, 20, and 21 of the Port Arthur port regulations. He reports that 97 supplementary Detailed Regulations covering nine pages were published in the Kwantung Government Gazette, but the consulate is translating only articles relevant to American shipping interests. Furthermore, Vincent reports that naval dry docks in the First Area operated by the Manchuria Dock Company (a South Manchuria Railway subsidiary) have had their operating lease renewed for another year, and that the naval station confirmed to the British Consul that foreign vessels may use the docks with permission from the Commander-in-Chief.
subfiles.title: Despatch from Consul John Carter Vincent to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew on Corrections to Port Arthur Regulations
